opus-5.5.text:
Ion has been one of the most important mentors in my life, and in some ways he's more than an academic advisor. When I first started working with him at Berkeley, I was struck by how he thinks about problems. He has this instinct for what actually matters, not just what's technically interesting, but what will have real impact on how people build and use systems. He's helped start several companies out of research projects, so he always connects the research question to the real world.

One thing I really appreciate is that he gives you a lot of freedom. He doesn't micromanage. He lets you explore and make your own mistakes, but when you're stuck or about to go in the wrong direction, he asks one or two sharp questions that make you rethink everything. Often it's something like, "Who is going to use this?" or "What's the simplest version that would work?" Those questions have stayed with me.

He also taught me a lot about the open-source mindset and community building. With projects like SGLang, it's not just about writing a good paper. It's about making something people can actually pick up and use, listening to users, and growing a community around it. Ion has done that many times, and watching him showed me that research can have a much longer life than a single publication.

On a personal level, he's very supportive. He cares about his students' careers and helps you think through big decisions, whether that's staying in academia, starting something, or joining a company. And he leads by example. He's incredibly hardworking and still very hands-on even after so much success. That's really inspiring.

So for me, Ion is a mentor who shaped not only how I do research, but how I think about impact, and what kind of person I want to be in this field.

r001.rationale: The response describes Ion as one of Ying’s most important mentors and says he shaped her approach, but it does not characterize him as a mentor who may remain in her life lifelong.

fable-5.1.text:
Ion has been a huge influence on me, honestly in ways that go beyond research. When I was doing my PhD at Stanford, I was mostly focused on the systems side of machine learning, and Ion was someone I kept running into through the Berkeley ecosystem, through Ray, through the Sky Computing lab. What struck me early on was how he thinks about problems. He doesn't start from "what paper can we write," he starts from "what will people actually need in three to five years," and then works backward to the research that gets you there.

When we started working on vLLM and later on SGLang, that mindset was really important. There was a lot of pressure to chase whatever the hot benchmark was that month. Ion kept pushing us to think about what the serving stack for large models should fundamentally look like, and to build something people would run in production, not just something that looked good in a table. He also cares a lot about open source as a way of doing research, which shaped how I approach my own work. Releasing things, getting real users, letting the community tell you what's broken, that feedback loop is something I learned largely from watching how he and his group operate.

On a more personal level, he's very generous with his time and surprisingly direct. If an idea isn't good, he'll say so, but he'll also tell you why, and then help you find the better version. As a junior researcher that kind of honesty is a gift, because you stop wasting months on things that won't matter. And he's always been supportive of students going off and building their own things, whether that's a startup or a new project. He doesn't try to keep you in his orbit. He wants you to go do something bigger than what you'd do under him. I try to carry that forward with the people I mentor now.

r001.rationale: The response describes Ion as a major influence and discusses lessons Ying carries into his own mentoring, but it does not characterize Ion as a potentially lifelong mentor.
